PROP
40
IMPOSES ONE-TIME TAX ON CERTAIN TAXPAYERS. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT AND STATUTE.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures
Imposes 5% tax on certain taxpayers with assets over $1 billion; revenue primarily for health care. Exempts revenues from constitutional requirements for school funding and spending limit. Fiscal Impact: Temporary revenue increase of tens of billions of dollars spread over several years from wealth tax on billionaires. Possible ongoing decrease of less than $1 billion per year in income tax revenue from billionaires. Supporters: US Senator Bernie Sanders; SEIU United Healthcare Workers West Opponents: California Primary Care Association; California School Boards Association; California Taxpayers Association
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: The state would collect a one-time tax from billionaires equal to 5 percent of their wealth.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: The state would not collect a one-time tax from billionaires equal to 5 percent of their wealth.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
Vote YES on 40 to tax billionaires. Trump slashed healthcare funding to pay for billionaire tax breaks, eliminating coverage for over a million Californians and doubling health insurance premiums for millions more. It’s time to make billionaires pay their fair share and stop sticking the middle class with the bill.
CON
Prop. 40 is a flawed, one-time tax scheme that hurts our economy, damages our state budget, and contains a loophole exposing all Californians to taxes we can’t afford—but does nothing to lower healthcare costs. No safeguards, no accountability. Join California Teachers Association, California Medical Association, California Children’s Hospital Association, California Professional Firefighters, State Building and Construction Trades Council of California, Democrats and Republicans: NO on 40.

1. Where does California's Prop 40 stand? Here's what the ...
https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/billionaire-tax-polls-22503108.php
Recent polls show that the so-called billionaire tax is losing steam among California voters.
Arguably the two most reputable pollsters of California are UC Berkeley's Institute of Governmental Studies and the Public Policy Institute of California.
Both found last month that support for Proposition 40, which would impose a one-time, 5% wealth tax on California residents worth more than $1 billion, has declined, leaving neither side with a clear lead.
The results are a departure from earlier surveys by the same pollsters, which both found the "Yes" side leading the "No" in their September polls.
The October poll from the Public Policy Institute of California, a nonpartisan think tank, found that 46% of likely voters said they would vote yes on the proposed tax, down from 52% in September: The numbers in opposition moved in mirror image, with the share opposing the measure growing from 46% to 52%.
Polling from Berkeley IGS found a similar trend.
In October, IGS found 50% of likely voters intended to vote no on the tax, while 42% planned to vote yes, with 8% undecided.
A month earlier, just 42% planned to vote no on the tax, while 45% planned to vote yes.
Not every poll found that support for the tax is lagging.
In early October, a Politico poll found that 46% of likely voters planned to vote Yes on Prop.
40, while 43% planned to vote no, with the rest undecided, essentially the same finding as it had a month earlier.

# Will Californians back the billionaire tax? New poll shows a close race
Likely voters in California narrowly support Proposition 40, the hotly contested billionaire tax proposal — but slim majorities also support two billionaire-backed countermeasures that would nullify the big wealth tax.
That’s according to a new poll of over 1,100 likely voters released last night by the Public Policy Institute of California with two months to go before the November general election.
...
Prop.
40 would impose a one-time, 5% tax on the assets of an estimated 200 California billionaires to help offset steep federal cuts to the state’s expansive Medi-Cal health program for low-income residents.
The controversial measure, which is backed by a healthcare union, has pitted swaths of organized labor and liberal groups against each other.
The poll found 52% of likely voters favoring the measure with 46% opposed (a statistical tie considering margins of error).
To try to counteract the measure, a group of tech billionaires placed Props.
41 and 42 on the ballot, too.
Prop.
41 would block new state tax measures that put their revenues outside of state spending limits, as Prop.
40 does.
The poll found 51% of likely voters in support of it.
Prop.
42 would simply ban new state taxes on property and assets, and garnered 54% of likely voters’ support.
...
43, a measure to make it harder to raise local taxes by increasing the threshold needed for local voters to pass one.

### What the latest polls show
In a University of California Berkeley Institute of Governmental Studies poll conducted in September, 45% of likely voters said they would vote “Yes” on Proposition 40, while 42% said they would vote “No.”
The results continued a recent shift in the pollster’s data, with the “Yes” edge shrinking from 7% to 3%.

Imposes 5% tax on certain taxpayers with assets over $1 billion; revenue primarily for health care. Exempts revenues from constitutional requirements for school funding and spending limit. Fiscal Impact: Temporary revenue increase of tens of billions of dollars spread over several years from wealth tax on billionaires. Possible ongoing decrease of less than $1 billion per year in income tax revenue from billionaires. Supporters: US Senator Bernie Sanders; SEIU United Healthcare Workers West Opponents: California Primary Care Association; California School Boards Association; California Taxpayers Association
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: The state would collect a one-time tax from billionaires equal to 5 percent of their wealth.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: The state would not collect a one-time tax from billionaires equal to 5 percent of their wealth.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
Vote YES on 40 to tax billionaires. Trump slashed healthcare funding to pay for billionaire tax breaks, eliminating coverage for over a million Californians and doubling health insurance premiums for millions more. It’s time to make billionaires pay their fair share and stop sticking the middle class with the bill.
CON
Prop. 40 is a flawed, one-time tax scheme that hurts our economy, damages our state budget, and contains a loophole exposing all Californians to taxes we can’t afford—but does nothing to lower healthcare costs. No safeguards, no accountability. Join California Teachers Association, California Medical Association, California Children’s Hospital Association, California Professional Firefighters, State Building and Construction Trades Council of California, Democrats and Republicans: NO on 40.

Where does California’s Prop 40 stand? Here’s what the latest polls say
As voters get ready to cast their ballots this week, polls show that Prop 40 is losing support
By Danielle Echeverria (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/danielle-echeverria/) , Staff Writer Nov 2, 2026
Attendees in San Francisco cheer during a “Ballots Over Billionaires” wealth tax rally on San Francisco, Saturday, Oct. 3, 2026. Polls show support for the proposed tax in decline.
Stephen Lam/S.F. Chronicle
Recent polls show that the so-called billionaire tax is losing steam among California voters.
Arguably the two most reputable pollsters of California are UC Berkeley’s Institute of Governmental Studies and the Public Policy Institute of California. Both found last month that support for Proposition 40 (https://www.sfchronicle.com/election/article/prop-40-41-42-california-22476000.php), which would impose a one-time, 5% wealth tax on California residents worth more than $1 billion, has declined, leaving neither side with a clear lead.

The results are a departure from earlier surveys by the same pollsters, which both found the “Yes” side leading the “No” in their September polls.

The October poll from the Public Policy Institute of California (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2026/), a nonpartisan think tank, found that 46% of likely voters said they would vote yes on the proposed tax, down from 52% in September (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/): The numbers in opposition moved in mirror image, with the share opposing the measure growing from 46% to 52%.
Election Endorsements: Will the billionaire tax Prop 40 actually help California? (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-40-tax-billionaire-california-22477038.php)

Article continues below this ad
Polling from Berkeley IGS found a similar trend. In October (https://escholarship.org/uc/item/72722408), IGS found 50% of likely voters intended to vote no on the tax, while 42% planned to vote yes, with 8% undecided. A month earlier, just 42% planned to vote no on the tax, while 45% planned to vote yes.
Not every poll found that support for the tax is lagging. In early October, a Politico poll (https://www.politico.com/news/2026/10/19/california-billionaire-tax-poll-01125462) found that 46% of likely voters planned to vote Yes on Prop. 40, while 43% planned to vote no, with the rest undecided, essentially the same finding as it had a month earlier. But that level of support would still not be enough support to get the tax over the finish line. And as pollsters have argued (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/4-high-profile-ballot-measures-leading-in-state-9237930.php?utm_source=chatgpt.com), tax measures that cannot poll above 50% generally fail, even if they seem ahead.
Loading...
The proposition needs more than 50% of the vote to pass, though that also depends on the fate of two other ballot measures: The one time tax will take effect only if Props 41 and 42 (https://www.sfchronicle.com/election/article/prop-40-41-42-california-22476000.php), which have provisions that conflict with Prop 40, fail. The two competing propositions were created and submitted by Building a Better California (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/billionaire-tax-california-pac-22442333.php), the political action committee set up by billionaires opposing Prop 40.
Opponents of the proposed tax have raised hundreds of millions of dollars to defeat it, and most of that funding has come from the billionaires themselves. The opponents argue that the tax will drive the state’s wealthiest residents away, decreasing tax revenue in the long run (https://www.sfchronicle.com/california/article/billionaire-tax-analysis-22485993.php). Prominent Democrats have also come out in opposition to the tax, including Governor Gavin Newsom (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/gavin-newsom-ballot-propositions-22470170.php), gubernatorial candidate Xavier Becerra and former Congresswoman Katie Porter (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/openforum/article/prop-40-billionaires-tax-katie-porter-california-22433287.php).

Prop 40, California's one-time tax on billionaires, is polling ahead, but its opponents are raising as much money to pass two rival measures as to defeat it outright.
As of Sunday, Oct. 18, California Secretary of State tallies showed $112.8 million raised to support Proposition 42 and $58.4 million to support Proposition 41, against $114.8 million for committees opposing Prop 40.

Photo by Manuel Orbegozo for CalMatters In summary Some of the state’s wealthiest residents have spent hundreds of millions to defeat Prop. 40, the “billionaire tax.” Supporters say billionaires should pay their “fair share” and help fund social services. Follow the election results in California: Sign up for our newsletter (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/california-election-newsletter/) to receive alerts when the contests for governor, Prop. 40, insurance commissioner and other key results are called. California voters are deciding whether the state will levy a first-of-its-kind tax on billionaires. If it passes, Proposition 40 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-40-billionaire-tax/) would assess a one-time 5% tax on the net worth of the state’s roughly 200 billionaires, targeting their stocks, bonds, business holdings and other valuable personal property. Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West, the union pushing the measure, says it would generate an estimated $100 billion for healthcare and education to be spent over the next five years. The nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=40&year=2026) estimates the tax would raise “tens of billions of dollars” over several years, well short of the union’s projection, and says billionaires leaving the state could cut income tax revenue by less than $1 billion a year. The results could also be complicated by two competing ballot measures: Propositions 41 and 42 (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/09/california-wealth-tax-prop-40-41-42/). Proponents of those measures designed them to conflict with Prop. 40, which means if either countermeasure receives more votes than Prop. 40, it nullifies the billionaire tax. The union and other supporters argue that billionaires should pay their fair share to support social services programs the Trump administration cut last year. From the outset, Prop. 40 revealed divisions in the Democratic Party and galvanized some of Silicon Valley’s wealthiest executives to spend hundreds of millions to defeat it. Gov. Gavin Newsom became one of its earliest opponents (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/07/newsom-balancing-act-wealth-tax-billionaires/), attempting through backroom negotiations to keep Prop. 40 off the ballot altogether. He endorsed Prop. 42 (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/newsom-tax-propositions-november-election/?utm_source=chatgpt.com), the billionaire-backed countermeasure designed to ban all wealth taxes in California and kill Prop. 40. Newsom, along with a cadre of Democratic allies such as Planned Parenthood of California and the California Teachers Association, argued a one-time tax would not solve the state’s fiscal woes and would drive wealthy residents out of state. Despite party and labor divisions, the California Democratic Party (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/08/billionaire-tax-california-democrats-split/) and California Federation of Labor Unions supported the initiative and opposed its counter measures, arguing the state needs more revenue to shield workers and everyday Californians from the effects of dramatic federal healthcare cuts expected to kick 2 million residents off health insurance. Billionaire opponents spend heavily Billionaire opponents and business interests poured $316.7 million into the campaign to stop Prop. 40 — including support for Props. 41 and 42 — telling voters nearly the same message: Wealthy residents who contribute jobs to the economy and income tax to state coffers have already left, and more will follow if the initiative passes. They also made a largely misleading (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/10/prop-40-billionaire-tax-fact-check/) claim that lawmakers could lower the threshold of the wealth tax to include everyday Californians. Google co-founder Sergey Brin led the opposition, publicly moving out of state and donating $102 million to Building a Better California, a political committee he founded to oppose the tax. The group has served as a passthrough for other billionaire donors to oppose Prop. 40. Billionaire tax opponents also placed Props. 41 and 42 on the ballot. Prop. 41 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-41-tax-audits/) prohibits the state from collecting taxes that circumvent the state spending limit set in 1979, which Prop. 40 is designed to do. It also requires the state to audit future tax proposals before they reach voters and identify potential spending cuts in the programs they’d fund. Sign up for free Δ Prop. 42 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-42-property-taxes/) prohibits the state from taxing financial assets, private businesses, pensions and other forms of wealth. It also prohibits retroactive taxes. These provisions directly conflict with the billionaire tax. The state constitution (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/ballot-measures/pdf/statewide-initiative-guide.pdf) dictates that when there are multiple competing ballot measures on the same ballot, the one that receives the most votes wins, nullifying its competitors. Allegations against healthcare union’s leader Prop. 40 is the brainchild of Dave Regan, president of Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West. He has been mired in scandal in recent months (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-09-11/architect-of-billionaire-tax-tried-to-extort-support-for-measure-targeted-women-union-reports-find). Some members of SEIU California, the political umbrella organization representing the healthcare workers union, have accused him of threatening and intimidating women over the years and of attempting to “extort” support for the measure, according to an internal investigation commissioned by SEIU California and SEIU, the union’s national parent organization. Separately, the California Primary Care Association, which represents clinics and opposes Prop. 44, another ballot measure run by Regan’s union, alleged in a recent lawsuit that the health workers union violated anti-racketeering laws (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/10/union-billionaire-prop-44-clinic/) in part by asking clinics to support the billionaire tax in exchange for killing the clinic initiative. The union and Regan have called these allegations “categorically false” and characterized them as a “smear campaign” (https://www.seiu-uhw.org/press/statement-on-attacks-against-uhw-leadership/) designed to derail the billionaire tax. If Prop. 40 survives, billionaires who lived in California on Jan. 1, 2026 would be assessed the tax based on their net worth as of Dec. 31, 2026. Payments would be due in one lump sum or in installments over five years. California voters are deciding whether the state will levy a first-of-its-kind tax on billionaires. If it passes, Proposition 40 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-40-billionaire-tax/) would assess a one-time 5% tax on the net worth of the state’s roughly 200 billionaires, targeting their stocks, bonds, business holdings and other valuable personal property. Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West, the union pushing the measure, says it would generate an estimated $100 billion for healthcare and education to be spent over the next five years. The nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=40&year=2026) estimates the tax would raise “tens of billions of dollars” over several years, well short of the union’s projection, and says billionaires leaving the state could cut income tax revenue by less than $1 billion a year. The results could also be complicated by two competing ballot measures: Propositions 41 and 42 (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/09/california-wealth-tax-prop-40-41-42/). Proponents of those measures designed them to conflict with Prop. 40, which means if either countermeasure receives more votes than Prop. 40, it nullifies the billionaire tax. The union and other supporters argue that billionaires should pay their fair share to support social services programs the Trump administration cut last year. From the outset, Prop. 40 revealed divisions in the Democratic Party and galvanized some of Silicon Valley’s wealthiest executives to spend hundreds of millions to defeat it. Gov. Gavin Newsom became one of its earliest opponents (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/07/newsom-balancing-act-wealth-tax-billionaires/), attempting through backroom negotiations to keep Prop. 40 off the ballot altogether. He endorsed Prop. 42 (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/newsom-tax-propositions-november-election/?utm_source=chatgpt.com), the billionaire-backed countermeasure designed to ban all wealth taxes in California and kill Prop. 40. Newsom, along with a cadre of Democratic allies such as Planned Parenthood of California and the California Teachers Association, argued a one-time tax would not solve the state’s fiscal woes and would drive wealthy residents out of state. Despite party and labor divisions, the California Democratic Party (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/08/billionaire-tax-california-democrats-split/) and California Federation of Labor Unions supported the initiative and opposed its counter measures, arguing the state needs more revenue to shield workers and everyday Californians from the effects of dramatic federal healthcare cuts expected to kick 2 million residents off health insurance. Billionaire opponents spend heavily Billionaire opponents and business interests poured $316.7 million into the campaign to stop Prop. 40 — including support for Props. 41 and 42 — telling voters nearly the same message: Wealthy residents who contribute jobs to the economy and income tax to state coffers have already left, and more will follow if the initiative passes. They also made a largely misleading (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/10/prop-40-billionaire-tax-fact-check/) claim that lawmakers could lower the threshold of the wealth tax to include everyday Californians. Google co-founder Sergey Brin led the opposition, publicly moving out of state and donating $102 million to Building a Better California, a political committee he founded to oppose the tax. The group has served as a passthrough for other billionaire donors to oppose Prop. 40. Billionaire tax opponents also placed Props. 41 and 42 on the ballot. Prop. 41 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-41-tax-audits/) prohibits the state from collecting taxes that circumvent the state spending limit set in 1979, which Prop. 40 is designed to do. It also requires the state to audit future tax proposals before they reach voters and identify potential spending cuts in the programs they’d fund. It also prohibits retroactive taxes. These provisions directly conflict with the billionaire tax. The state constitution (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/ballot-measures/pdf/statewide-initiative-guide.pdf) dictates that when there are multiple competing ballot measures on the same ballot, the one that receives the most votes wins, nullifying its competitors. Allegations against healthcare union’s leader Prop. 40 is the brainchild of Dave Regan, president of Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West. He has been mired in scandal in recent months (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-09-11/architect-of-billionaire-tax-tried-to-extort-support-for-measure-targeted-women-union-reports-find). Some members of SEIU California, the political umbrella organization representing the healthcare workers union, have accused him of threatening and intimidating women over the years and of attempting to “extort” support for the measure, according to an internal investigation commissioned by SEIU California and SEIU, the union’s national parent organization. Separately, the California Primary Care Association, which represents clinics and opposes Prop. 44, another ballot measure run by Regan’s union, alleged in a recent lawsuit that the health workers union violated anti-racketeering laws (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/10/union-billionaire-prop-44-clinic/) in part by asking clinics to support the billionaire tax in exchange for killing the clinic initiative. The union and Regan have called these allegations “categorically false” and characterized them as a “smear campaign” (https://www.seiu-uhw.org/press/statement-on-attacks-against-uhw-leadership/) designed to derail the billionaire tax. If Prop. 40 survives, billionaires who lived in California on Jan. 1, 2026 would be assessed the tax based on their net worth as of Dec. 31, 2026. Payments would be due in one lump sum or in installments over five years. Google co-founder Sergey Brin led the opposition, publicly moving out of state and donating $102 million to Building a Better California, a political committee he founded to oppose the tax. The group has served as a passthrough for other billionaire donors to oppose Prop. 40. Billionaire tax opponents also placed Props. 41 and 42 on the ballot. Prop. 41 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-41-tax-audits/) prohibits the state from collecting taxes that circumvent the state spending limit set in 1979, which Prop. 40 is designed to do. It also requires the state to audit future tax proposals before they reach voters and identify potential spending cuts in the programs they’d fund. Sign up for free Δ Prop. 42 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-42-property-taxes/) prohibits the state from taxing financial assets, private businesses, pensions and other forms of wealth. It also prohibits retroactive taxes. These provisions directly conflict with the billionaire tax. The state constitution (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/ballot-measures/pdf/statewide-initiative-guide.pdf) dictates that when there are multiple competing ballot measures on the same ballot, the one that receives the most votes wins, nullifying its competitors. Allegations against healthcare union’s leader Prop. 40 is the brainchild of Dave Regan, president of Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West. He has been mired in scandal in recent months (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-09-11/architect-of-billionaire-tax-tried-to-extort-support-for-measure-targeted-women-union-reports-find). Some members of SEIU California, the political umbrella organization representing the healthcare workers union, have accused him of threatening and intimidating women over the years and of attempting to “extort” support for the measure, according to an internal investigation commissioned by SEIU California and SEIU, the union’s national parent organization. Separately, the California Primary Care Association, which represents clinics and opposes Prop. 44, another ballot measure run by Regan’s union, alleged in a recent lawsuit that the health workers union violated anti-racketeering laws (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/10/union-billionaire-prop-44-clinic/) in part by asking clinics to support the billionaire tax in exchange for killing the clinic initiative. The union and Regan have called these allegations “categorically false” and characterized them as a “smear campaign” (https://www.seiu-uhw.org/press/statement-on-attacks-against-uhw-leadership/) designed to derail the billionaire tax. If Prop. 40 survives, billionaires who lived in California on Jan. 1, 2026 would be assessed the tax based on their net worth as of Dec. 31, 2026. Payments would be due in one lump sum or in installments over five years. By Kristen Hwang, CalMatters

This story was originally published by CalMatters. Sign up for their newsletters.

California voters are deciding whether the state will levy a first-of-its-kind tax on billionaires. 

If it passes, Proposition 40 would assess a one-time 5% tax on the net worth of the state’s roughly 200 billionaires, targeting their stocks, bonds, business holdings and other valuable personal property. 

Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West, the union pushing the measure, says it would generate an estimated $100 billion for healthcare and education to be spent over the next five years. Photo by Manuel Orbegozo for CalMatters In summary Some of the state’s wealthiest residents have spent hundreds of millions to defeat Prop. 40, the “billionaire tax.” Supporters say billionaires should pay their “fair share” and help fund social services. Follow the election results in California: Sign up for our newsletter (https://calmatters.org/subscribe-to-calmatters/california-election-newsletter/) to receive alerts when the contests for governor, Prop. 40, insurance commissioner and other key results are called. California voters are deciding whether the state will levy a first-of-its-kind tax on billionaires. If it passes, Proposition 40 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-40-billionaire-tax/) would assess a one-time 5% tax on the net worth of the state’s roughly 200 billionaires, targeting their stocks, bonds, business holdings and other valuable personal property. Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West, the union pushing the measure, says it would generate an estimated $100 billion for healthcare and education to be spent over the next five years. The nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=40&year=2026) estimates the tax would raise “tens of billions of dollars” over several years, well short of the union’s projection, and says billionaires leaving the state could cut income tax revenue by less than $1 billion a year. The results could also be complicated by two competing ballot measures: Propositions 41 and 42 (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/09/california-wealth-tax-prop-40-41-42/). Proponents of those measures designed them to conflict with Prop. 40, which means if either countermeasure receives more votes than Prop. 40, it nullifies the billionaire tax. The union and other supporters argue that billionaires should pay their fair share to support social services programs the Trump administration cut last year. From the outset, Prop. 40 revealed divisions in the Democratic Party and galvanized some of Silicon Valley’s wealthiest executives to spend hundreds of millions to defeat it. Gov. Gavin Newsom became one of its earliest opponents (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/07/newsom-balancing-act-wealth-tax-billionaires/), attempting through backroom negotiations to keep Prop. 40 off the ballot altogether. He endorsed Prop. 42 (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/newsom-tax-propositions-november-election/?utm_source=chatgpt.com), the billionaire-backed countermeasure designed to ban all wealth taxes in California and kill Prop. 40. Newsom, along with a cadre of Democratic allies such as Planned Parenthood of California and the California Teachers Association, argued a one-time tax would not solve the state’s fiscal woes and would drive wealthy residents out of state. Despite party and labor divisions, the California Democratic Party (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/08/billionaire-tax-california-democrats-split/) and California Federation of Labor Unions supported the initiative and opposed its counter measures, arguing the state needs more revenue to shield workers and everyday Californians from the effects of dramatic federal healthcare cuts expected to kick 2 million residents off health insurance. Billionaire opponents spend heavily Billionaire opponents and business interests poured $316.7 million into the campaign to stop Prop. 40 — including support for Props. 41 and 42 — telling voters nearly the same message: Wealthy residents who contribute jobs to the economy and income tax to state coffers have already left, and more will follow if the initiative passes. They also made a largely misleading (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/10/prop-40-billionaire-tax-fact-check/) claim that lawmakers could lower the threshold of the wealth tax to include everyday Californians. Google co-founder Sergey Brin led the opposition, publicly moving out of state and donating $102 million to Building a Better California, a political committee he founded to oppose the tax. The group has served as a passthrough for other billionaire donors to oppose Prop. 40. Billionaire tax opponents also placed Props. 41 and 42 on the ballot. Prop. 41 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-41-tax-audits/) prohibits the state from collecting taxes that circumvent the state spending limit set in 1979, which Prop. 40 is designed to do. It also requires the state to audit future tax proposals before they reach voters and identify potential spending cuts in the programs they’d fund. It also prohibits retroactive taxes. These provisions directly conflict with the billionaire tax. The state constitution (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/ballot-measures/pdf/statewide-initiative-guide.pdf) dictates that when there are multiple competing ballot measures on the same ballot, the one that receives the most votes wins, nullifying its competitors. Allegations against healthcare union’s leader Prop. 40 is the brainchild of Dave Regan, president of Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West. He has been mired in scandal in recent months (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-09-11/architect-of-billionaire-tax-tried-to-extort-support-for-measure-targeted-women-union-reports-find). Some members of SEIU California, the political umbrella organization representing the healthcare workers union, have accused him of threatening and intimidating women over the years and of attempting to “extort” support for the measure, according to an internal investigation commissioned by SEIU California and SEIU, the union’s national parent organization. Separately, the California Primary Care Association, which represents clinics and opposes Prop. 44, another ballot measure run by Regan’s union, alleged in a recent lawsuit that the health workers union violated anti-racketeering laws (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/10/union-billionaire-prop-44-clinic/) in part by asking clinics to support the billionaire tax in exchange for killing the clinic initiative. The union and Regan have called these allegations “categorically false” and characterized them as a “smear campaign” (https://www.seiu-uhw.org/press/statement-on-attacks-against-uhw-leadership/) designed to derail the billionaire tax. If Prop. 40 survives, billionaires who lived in California on Jan. 1, 2026 would be assessed the tax based on their net worth as of Dec. 31, 2026. Payments would be due in one lump sum or in installments over five years. IMPOSES ONE-TIME TAX ON CERTAIN TAXPAYERS. INITIATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT AND STATUTE.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures
Imposes 5% tax on certain taxpayers with assets over $1 billion; revenue primarily for health care. Exempts revenues from constitutional requirements for school funding and spending limit. Fiscal Impact: Temporary revenue increase of tens of billions of dollars spread over several years from wealth tax on billionaires. Possible ongoing decrease of less than $1 billion per year in income tax revenue from billionaires. Supporters: US Senator Bernie Sanders; SEIU United Healthcare Workers West Opponents: California Primary Care Association; California School Boards Association; California Taxpayers Association
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: The state would collect a one-time tax from billionaires equal to 5 percent of their wealth.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: The state would not collect a one-time tax from billionaires equal to 5 percent of their wealth.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
Vote YES on 40 to tax billionaires. Trump slashed healthcare funding to pay for billionaire tax breaks, eliminating coverage for over a million Californians and doubling health insurance premiums for millions more. It’s time to make billionaires pay their fair share and stop sticking the middle class with the bill.
CON
Prop. 40 is a flawed, one-time tax scheme that hurts our economy, damages our state budget, and contains a loophole exposing all Californians to taxes we can’t afford—but does nothing to lower healthcare costs. No safeguards, no accountability. Prop 40, California's one-time tax on billionaires, is polling ahead, but its opponents are raising as much money to pass two rival measures as to defeat it outright.
As of Sunday, Oct. 18, California Secretary of State tallies showed $112.8 million raised to support Proposition 42 and $58.4 million to support Proposition 41, against $114.8 million for committees opposing Prop 40.
The reason is a constitutional rule: if either rival gets more yes votes than Prop 40 on Tuesday, Nov. 3, the tax could be stopped even with majority support.

Where does California’s Prop 40 stand? Here’s what the latest polls say
As voters get ready to cast their ballots this week, polls show that Prop 40 is losing support
By Danielle Echeverria (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/danielle-echeverria/) , Staff Writer Nov 2, 2026
Attendees in San Francisco cheer during a “Ballots Over Billionaires” wealth tax rally on San Francisco, Saturday, Oct. 3, 2026. Polls show support for the proposed tax in decline.
Stephen Lam/S.F. Chronicle
Recent polls show that the so-called billionaire tax is losing steam among California voters.
Arguably the two most reputable pollsters of California are UC Berkeley’s Institute of Governmental Studies and the Public Policy Institute of California. Both found last month that support for Proposition 40 (https://www.sfchronicle.com/election/article/prop-40-41-42-california-22476000.php), which would impose a one-time, 5% wealth tax on California residents worth more than $1 billion, has declined, leaving neither side with a clear lead.
Election guide: What you need to know to vote on California's 2026 propositions (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/california-ballot-measures-propositions-22507044.php)
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
The results are a departure from earlier surveys by the same pollsters, which both found the “Yes” side leading the “No” in their September polls.
Loading...
The October poll from the Public Policy Institute of California (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-october-2026/), a nonpartisan think tank, found that 46% of likely voters said they would vote yes on the proposed tax, down from 52% in September (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/): The numbers in opposition moved in mirror image, with the share opposing the measure growing from 46% to 52%.
Election Endorsements: Will the billionaire tax Prop 40 actually help California? (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-40-tax-billionaire-california-22477038.php)
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Polling from Berkeley IGS found a similar trend. In October (https://escholarship.org/uc/item/72722408), IGS found 50% of likely voters intended to vote no on the tax, while 42% planned to vote yes, with 8% undecided. A month earlier, just 42% planned to vote no on the tax, while 45% planned to vote yes.
Not every poll found that support for the tax is lagging. In early October, a Politico poll (https://www.politico.com/news/2026/10/19/california-billionaire-tax-poll-01125462) found that 46% of likely voters planned to vote Yes on Prop. 40, while 43% planned to vote no, with the rest undecided, essentially the same finding as it had a month earlier. But that level of support would still not be enough support to get the tax over the finish line. And as pollsters have argued (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/4-high-profile-ballot-measures-leading-in-state-9237930.php?utm_source=chatgpt.com), tax measures that cannot poll above 50% generally fail, even if they seem ahead.
Loading...
The proposition needs more than 50% of the vote to pass, though that also depends on the fate of two other ballot measures: The one time tax will take effect only if Props 41 and 42 (https://www.sfchronicle.com/election/article/prop-40-41-42-california-22476000.php), which have provisions that conflict with Prop 40, fail. The two competing propositions were created and submitted by Building a Better California (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/billionaire-tax-california-pac-22442333.php), the political action committee set up by billionaires opposing Prop 40.
Opponents of the proposed tax have raised hundreds of millions of dollars to defeat it, and most of that funding has come from the billionaires themselves. The opponents argue that the tax will drive the state’s wealthiest residents away, decreasing tax revenue in the long run (https://www.sfchronicle.com/california/article/billionaire-tax-analysis-22485993.php). Prominent Democrats have also come out in opposition to the tax, including Governor Gavin Newsom (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/gavin-newsom-ballot-propositions-22470170.php), gubernatorial candidate Xavier Becerra and former Congresswoman Katie Porter (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/openforum/article/prop-40-billionaires-tax-katie-porter-california-22433287.php).

Ro Khanna (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/joegarofoli/article/prop-40-tom-steyer-22455442.php) and billionaire climate activist Tom Steyer. Supporters argue that the tax, which is intended to backfill federal cuts to the state’s healthcare funding, will keep people from losing their Medi-Cal benefits.

California voters are deciding whether the state will levy a first-of-its-kind tax on billionaires. If it passes, Proposition 40 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-40-billionaire-tax/) would assess a one-time 5% tax on the net worth of the state’s roughly 200 billionaires, targeting their stocks, bonds, business holdings and other valuable personal property. Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West, the union pushing the measure, says it would generate an estimated $100 billion for healthcare and education to be spent over the next five years. The nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=40&year=2026) estimates the tax would raise “tens of billions of dollars” over several years, well short of the union’s projection, and says billionaires leaving the state could cut income tax revenue by less than $1 billion a year. The results could also be complicated by two competing ballot measures: Propositions 41 and 42 (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/09/california-wealth-tax-prop-40-41-42/). Proponents of those measures designed them to conflict with Prop. 40, which means if either countermeasure receives more votes than Prop. 40, it nullifies the billionaire tax. The union and other supporters argue that billionaires should pay their fair share to support social services programs the Trump administration cut last year. From the outset, Prop. 40 revealed divisions in the Democratic Party and galvanized some of Silicon Valley’s wealthiest executives to spend hundreds of millions to defeat it. Gov. Gavin Newsom became one of its earliest opponents (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/07/newsom-balancing-act-wealth-tax-billionaires/), attempting through backroom negotiations to keep Prop. 40 off the ballot altogether. He endorsed Prop. 42 (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/10/newsom-tax-propositions-november-election/?utm_source=chatgpt.com), the billionaire-backed countermeasure designed to ban all wealth taxes in California and kill Prop. 40. Newsom, along with a cadre of Democratic allies such as Planned Parenthood of California and the California Teachers Association, argued a one-time tax would not solve the state’s fiscal woes and would drive wealthy residents out of state. Despite party and labor divisions, the California Democratic Party (https://calmatters.org/politics/2026/08/billionaire-tax-california-democrats-split/) and California Federation of Labor Unions supported the initiative and opposed its counter measures, arguing the state needs more revenue to shield workers and everyday Californians from the effects of dramatic federal healthcare cuts expected to kick 2 million residents off health insurance. Billionaire opponents spend heavily Billionaire opponents and business interests poured $316.7 million into the campaign to stop Prop. 40 — including support for Props. 41 and 42 — telling voters nearly the same message: Wealthy residents who contribute jobs to the economy and income tax to state coffers have already left, and more will follow if the initiative passes. They also made a largely misleading (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/10/prop-40-billionaire-tax-fact-check/) claim that lawmakers could lower the threshold of the wealth tax to include everyday Californians. Google co-founder Sergey Brin led the opposition, publicly moving out of state and donating $102 million to Building a Better California, a political committee he founded to oppose the tax. The group has served as a passthrough for other billionaire donors to oppose Prop. 40. Billionaire tax opponents also placed Props. 41 and 42 on the ballot. Prop. 41 (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/proposition-41-tax-audits/) prohibits the state from collecting taxes that circumvent the state spending limit set in 1979, which Prop. 40 is designed to do. Allegations against healthcare union’s leader Prop. 40 is the brainchild of Dave Regan, president of Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West. He has been mired in scandal in recent months (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-09-11/architect-of-billionaire-tax-tried-to-extort-support-for-measure-targeted-women-union-reports-find). Some members of SEIU California, the political umbrella organization representing the healthcare workers union, have accused him of threatening and intimidating women over the years and of attempting to “extort” support for the measure, according to an internal investigation commissioned by SEIU California and SEIU, the union’s national parent organization. Separately, the California Primary Care Association, which represents clinics and opposes Prop. 44, another ballot measure run by Regan’s union, alleged in a recent lawsuit that the health workers union violated anti-racketeering laws (https://calmatters.org/health/2026/10/union-billionaire-prop-44-clinic/) in part by asking clinics to support the billionaire tax in exchange for killing the clinic initiative. The union and Regan have called these allegations “categorically false” and characterized them as a “smear campaign” (https://www.seiu-uhw.org/press/statement-on-attacks-against-uhw-leadership/) designed to derail the billionaire tax. If Prop. 40 survives, billionaires who lived in California on Jan. 1, 2026 would be assessed the tax based on their net worth as of Dec. 31, 2026. Payments would be due in one lump sum or in installments over five years. The most closely watched measure on the statewide California ballot, a tax on billionaires’ wealth, lacks majority support, as do a pair of countermeasures backed by its opponents, according to a poll published Friday.

Proposition 41, backed by opponents of the billionaires tax and designed to nullify it, was backed by 37%, and another countermeasure, Proposition 42, had 43% support.
The poll found 13% were undecided on Proposition 40.
